demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Negative Appraisals.value: I should have protected others and I failed
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'I have no future' is a broad, severe hopelessness appraisal, while 'others can see what happened to me just by looking at me' implies a visible stigma/marked external sign. For a trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another, the latter is hard to justify clinically unless there is disfigurement or public exposure, neither of which is represented elsewhere.

issues.item: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: For a male delivery driver whose trauma was accidentally causing serious injury to another person, the appraisal that others can visibly see what happened to him by looking at him is hard to reconcile with the trauma type unless there are visible injuries or marked stigma, which are not otherwise represented. The other selected appraisals centre on guilt and responsibility, so this item pulls toward a different formulation theme and is not well aligned with the otherwise coherent guilt-based negative appraisal pattern.

vignette:
Arjun Patel is a 34-year-old married delivery driver who came to treatment months after a road accident in which another person was seriously injured. He speaks about the event carefully and with visible strain, returning again and again to the same conclusion: that it happened because of the way he acted. On the day of the accident, he was working his usual route, moving between apartment buildings and storefronts in his delivery van. In his account, the moment has become painfully narrow and exacting. He remembers a routine stop, a turn, a person in the road, and the sickening instant when he understood that his vehicle had hit someone. What has stayed with him most is not only that another person was badly hurt, but that he was the one behind the wheel when it happened. Since then, he has not been able to hold the event as a terrible accident alone; he has come to see it as evidence of a personal failure.

In the first sessions, Arjun does not describe himself as unlucky or overwhelmed. He describes himself as responsible. He says, in different forms, that he should have protected other people and that he failed. The injury to the other person feels to him like proof that he did not do the one thing he was supposed to do while driving for work: keep others safe. He speaks about the job in moral terms rather than practical ones. Delivering packages means being on neighborhood streets all day, near pedestrians, cyclists, children getting out of cars, older people crossing slowly. For him, that reality has sharpened his judgment of himself. He believes he was in a position where vigilance was required, and because someone was seriously hurt, he concludes that he failed in that duty.

This belief has taken on the force of a lasting verdict. Arjun says he will never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened. He goes over the event with a punishing kind of hindsight, asking what else he could have done in those seconds and treating every imagined alternative as something he should have managed. In his telling, there is no allowance for the confusion and speed of the moment. He focuses instead on not having prevented the injury, as if there must have been one decisive action that would have changed everything if only he had taken it. The part he cannot put down is the sense of inaction: not merely that something terrible happened, but that he did not do enough, fast enough, well enough.

At work, this has changed how he moves through ordinary days. He still encounters the same settings that now carry the meaning of what happened: residential corners, parking lots, people stepping off curbs while he is trying to complete a route. The daily environment of delivery driving has become the place where his self-judgment is continually rehearsed. When he describes passing through crowded streets, what stands out is not fear in a broad sense but a relentless accusation directed at himself. He watches his own driving as though looking for evidence that he is the kind of person who causes harm. A pedestrian near the van, a sudden movement at a crosswalk, even the need to make a careful turn into a tight space can bring him back to the same conclusion that the accident happened because of the way he acted. His workday has become saturated with reminders of his responsibility and, in his mind, his failure.

At home with his wife, Arjun has become harder to reassure. When she tells him it was an accident, he does not feel comforted; he feels misunderstood. From his perspective, calling it an accident risks excusing something he sees as morally inexcusable. He does not argue loudly about this, but he returns to it quietly and persistently, as if keeping the blame fixed on himself is the only honest position. What pains him most is the thought that another person is living with serious injury while he goes on with his routines. That contrast deepens his conviction that he should have done more and that he has no right to let himself move past it.

By the time he sought help, Arjun seemed exhausted by the constancy of this internal judgment. He was not coming in to say that he felt shaken in a vague way; he was coming in because he felt condemned by his own mind. He wanted help because he could no longer imagine how to live with the belief that he failed to protect someone and caused irreversible harm through his actions. What he fears most is that this says something permanent about him—that he is, at his core, someone who cannot be trusted to keep other people safe. What he hopes for, though he says it cautiously, is not to be let off the hook, but to understand whether it is possible to remember what happened without spending the rest of his life unforgiving himself.
